opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think compression is actually one of the most useful lenses for understanding what these models are doing and why they behave differently from Transformers.

The basic picture is this: a state space model, or any recurrent model, processes a sequence one step at a time and maintains a fixed-size hidden state. That state is essentially a compressed summary of everything the model has seen so far. At every step it has to decide what to keep, what to throw away, and how to fold the new input into what it already has. So the whole model is fundamentally a compression machine. Its quality depends on how well it can squeeze the relevant history into a bounded amount of memory.

Contrast that with attention. A Transformer doesn't compress at all, in a sense. It keeps the full KV cache, every token's representation, and at each step it can look back over all of it. That's why it's so good at things like exact recall or copying, and it's also why it's expensive. Memory grows linearly with the sequence and computation grows quadratically. So you can think of the two as sitting at opposite ends of a spectrum: attention is like a perfect cache with no compression, and SSMs are a fully compressed state.

The question then becomes: if you're going to compress, what's the *optimal* way to do it? That idea actually goes back to some of my earliest work on this line, like HiPPO, where the question was literally, given a continuous stream of input, how do you maintain an optimal online approximation of the history in a fixed number of coefficients? That gave us principled ways to initialize and structure the state matrices, projecting the past onto orthogonal polynomial bases and so on. That's the mathematical origin of S4.

What changed with Mamba was recognizing that good compression isn't just about approximating the signal uniformly well. It's about being *selective*. Language and most real data are full of things you should forget and a few things you really need to remember. A linear time-invariant system treats every input the same way, so it can't make content-dependent decisions about what matters. Making the dynamics input-dependent, the selection mechanism, is really what lets the model compress intelligently, filtering out noise and holding onto the important information. In my view, that's the key ingredient for an SSM to be competitive on things like language.

I also think compression connects to a broader view of intelligence. There's a long-standing idea that learning *is* compression, that finding structure in data means finding a shorter description of it. A model that's forced to build a compact, abstract state may be learning something closer to an actual understanding, versus one that can always just go look things up in the cache. Of course, that's also the weakness: if you compress, you'll sometimes lose a detail you later needed, and that's exactly where SSMs struggle relative to attention on precise retrieval tasks.

That's why I don't see it as one versus the other. Hybrid models that interleave a few attention layers with mostly SSM layers seem to get the best of both: the efficient, compressed, long-range state from the SSM, plus a small amount of exact memory from attention when you really need it. And framing everything in terms of compression helps you reason about those tradeoffs: how big the state should be, what should be cached, and where the model should be allowed to forget.

r001.rationale: The response says an SSM must choose what to keep or discard and frames its quality around compressing relevant history into bounded memory, alongside attention’s higher memory and compute costs.

r002.rationale: It says attention preserves the full cache and supports exact recall, but does not state that some tasks require retaining the entire history or that this limits compression.

r003.rationale: It says compression can lose a detail that is later needed, communicating that discarded information is no longer available from the compressed state.

r004.rationale: The response describes selective, input-dependent dynamics, but does not express hope that training on sufficient, appropriate data will teach the model what information to encode.

r005.rationale: It favors hybrids for combining efficient SSM state with exact memory when needed, but does not attribute interest in hybrids to tasks requiring retention of the complete history.

r006.rationale: It characterizes attention as a perfect cache that keeps every token’s representation and can look back over all of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think compression is really the right lens for understanding what a state space model is doing, and honestly for understanding the whole design space of sequence models.

The basic framing is this. Any autoregressive model has to take everything it's seen so far and turn it into some state that it uses to predict what comes next. The question is just what that state looks like. Attention, in a sense, refuses to compress. It keeps the entire history around as a KV cache, and that's why it's so good at precise recall, but it's also why it scales badly. Every token you generate costs you something proportional to the whole context. On the other end, a recurrent model, including an SSM, has a fixed-size state. So it's forced to compress. It has to decide, at every step, what's worth keeping and what to throw away.

Once you see it that way, the design problem becomes very clear. The quality of the model is basically the quality of its compression. A fixed-size state is only a limitation if you're compressing badly. So the question I kept asking myself was, how do you make the compression as close to optimal as possible for the data you actually care about?

That's really what motivated the move from S4 to Mamba. S4 and the earlier models were linear time-invariant, so the way they updated the state didn't depend on the input. That's like a compression scheme that treats every token identically. It works great for things like audio or continuous signals where the information is smooth and spread out. But for language, that's a terrible assumption. Some tokens matter a lot and some matter very little, and you need the model to be able to look at an input and say, this one I should store, this one I should basically ignore. So selectivity is really about making the compression input-dependent, letting the model allocate its limited state budget to the things that are actually informative.

And I'd push the point a bit further. I think the interesting regime isn't "compress everything" versus "compress nothing." It's that different kinds of information want different treatment. There's a lot of content in a sequence that's redundant or highly predictable, and you should compress that aggressively. And then there's a smaller amount that needs to be recalled exactly, like a name or a number, and attention is genuinely better at that. So I don't see this as SSMs replacing attention. I think of it as, a good architecture should be spending its memory where the information is, and that naturally leads you toward hybrids, where most layers are doing efficient compressed state tracking and a few layers are doing precise retrieval.

The other thing that I find really appealing about the compression view is that it connects to how we think about intelligence more generally. Understanding something is, in a sense, finding a short description of it. A model that can hold a conversation in a small fixed state isn't doing that because it memorized the transcript. It's doing it because it built an abstraction of what's going on. So when I think about where these models should go, I'm less interested in just making the state bigger, and more interested in making it smarter about what it chooses to remember.

r001.rationale: The response says SSMs must decide what to keep and discard, and describes selectivity as allocating limited state to informative inputs to improve compression.

r002.rationale: It says attention preserves the history and that some details need exact recall, but does not state that some tasks require retaining the entire history.

r003.rationale: The response describes compression and discarding information, but does not say that discarded information cannot later be retrieved from the state.

r004.rationale: It does not express hope that training on sufficient, appropriate data will teach an SSM what information matters.

r005.rationale: It favors hybrids for efficient state tracking plus precise retrieval, but does not attribute that interest to tasks requiring the complete history.

r006.rationale: It says attention keeps the history and is good at precise recall, but does not characterize its memorization of context as perfect.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as asking: what information from the past do you need to keep in order to do something useful in the future? A state space model takes a sequence and compresses everything it’s seen into a fixed-size state. So the central question is what that state should remember and what it can afford to forget.

Of course, “optimal” depends on your objective. If you want to reconstruct the history, that gives you one notion of a good compression. If you want to predict the next token, you might need a very different summary. Something that occurred a long time ago could matter more than most of the recent context.

So I see compression as a useful guiding principle for designing the state and its update rule. You want a representation that preserves the relevant information, and you want to be able to update it efficiently as new inputs arrive. The challenge is making that compression selective enough for the task without losing the computational advantages of a fixed-size state.

r001.rationale: It makes choosing what the state remembers central and says the summary should preserve task-relevant information while retaining fixed-size computational advantages.

r002.rationale: It mentions history reconstruction as one possible objective, but does not state that some tasks require keeping the entire history or that this limits compression.

r003.rationale: It discusses what the model may forget, but does not say discarded information cannot later be retrieved from the state.

r004.rationale: It does not mention training data teaching the model which information to encode.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss hybrids of stateful models and vanilla attention or link them to retaining complete history.

r006.rationale: It does not characterize vanilla attention as perfectly memorizing its context.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compression is a useful way to think about what the state is supposed to do. You’ve seen this whole sequence of inputs, and you have to summarize it in a fixed-size state. The question is: what information should you keep so that you can use it later?

And “optimal” depends on what you’re trying to do. You don’t necessarily want to reconstruct every input equally well. You want to preserve the information that matters for predicting the future or solving the task. But you generally don’t know ahead of time what that information is.

One approach that motivated our work was to start with a concrete mathematical problem: can we maintain a good approximation of the history of a signal as it streams in? If you represent that history using a set of basis functions, you can derive rules for updating the representation without storing the entire history. That gives you a principled starting point for the state space model.

Then learning can adapt that representation to the data. So I’d think of compression as a guiding principle for designing the memory: what gets remembered, what gets forgotten, and how efficiently can you update it?

r001.rationale: It frames the state as a fixed-size summary and asks what information to retain for future prediction or the task, while also emphasizing efficient updates.

r002.rationale: It does not say that some tasks require retaining the entire history or that this limits compression.

r003.rationale: It mentions what gets forgotten but does not state that discarded information cannot later be retrieved from the state.

r004.rationale: It says learning can adapt the representation to data, but does not express the specified hope about sufficient, appropriate training data teaching the model what to encode.

r005.rationale: It does not mention hybrid models or tasks requiring complete-history retention.

r006.rationale: It does not characterize vanilla attention as perfectly memorizing the model's context.
